gloss: Georgia (a medieval country in the South Caucasus, approximately coextensive with modern Georgia)
etymology: From Middle French Georgie, from Medieval Latin Geōrgia, from Persian گرج (gorj) (with influence from (sanctus) Geōrgius (“Saint George”)), from Middle Persian 𐭥𐭫𐭥𐭰𐭠𐭭 pl (Wiruz-ān, “Iberians, Georgians”), of unknown origin.
Borrowed from Anglo-Norman baraing, baraigne (continental Old French brehaigne), of unknown origin, but perhaps borrowed from a Germanic language, from Frankish *baʀ (“bare, naked”).

Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃-?
Proto-Germanic *blōþą
Proto-West Germanic *blōd
Old English blōd
Middle English blood
From Old English blōd, from Proto-West Germanic *blōd, from Proto-Germanic *blōþą, of uncertain origin.

gloss: a young bird, a bird in general
etymology: From Old English bridd, of disputed origin.

Inherited from Old English dile, from Proto-Germanic *deliz (“sow thistle”), an indigenous herb of uncertain origin; possibly Proto-Indo-European *dʰelh₁- (“sprout, bloom”) (Albanian dal, Middle Irish duille) or from a substrate.

gloss: an ordinary dog, especially a hunting dog
etymology: From Old English dogga, variant of docga, of unknown origin. See dog for more.

gloss: identical in amount, extent, or portion
etymology: Borrowed from Latin aequālis, of unknown origin. Doublet of egal.

gloss: Form; the shape or appearance of something:; A representation, likeness or depiction.
etymology:
Borrowed from Old French forme, fourme, from Latin fōrma, of unclear origin.
Pronunciations with /u/, /uː/ respectively reflect differing adaptations of Old French, while those with /ɔ/ are influenced by Latin fōrma; for possible differentiation in pronunciation by sense, see the usage note at Modern English form.

gloss: Entertainment or an instance of it; that which is enjoyable:; A sport or other outdoor or physical activity.
etymology:
Etymology tree
Proto-Germanic *gamaną
Proto-West Germanic *gaman
Old English gamen
Middle English game
From Old English gamen /gomen, from Proto-West Germanic *gaman, from Proto-Germanic *gamaną, of disputed origin.

gloss: A lance or spear; a polearm with a blade attached to the head.
etymology: Borrowed from Old French glaive, from Late Latin glā̆vus, of unclear origin.
From Anglo-Norman hidous, of uncertain origin. See English hideous for more.
Borrowed from Old French ahuge, a form of ahoge, of unknown origin.

gloss: To hurt (cause an injury or disease)
etymology: Usually taken to be an early borrowing from Old Northern French hurter, of disputed origin (with Old French /y/ thus developing like Old English /y/), but possibly instead from an Old English *hyrtan. In any case, equivalent to hurt + -en (infinitival suffix).

gloss: Something of great monetary worth or value, especially when made of gems:; An item of jewelry; a piece of personal ornamentation.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman juel; akin to Old French jouel, of disputed origin.

gloss: The near-white winter hide or fur of the least weasel; lettice.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman letuse; further etymology unknown.

gloss: A set of boughs, branches, or cuttings.
etymology: From Medieval Latin loppa, of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Old English *lopp, related to Norwegian lopa, lopna (“to become loosened by moisture”).

gloss: The appletree (Malus domestica) or its fruit.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin mālum, from Ancient Greek μῆλον (mêlon), of unknown origin.
From Old French mater (“to kill”), from Vulgar Latin *mattō, of disputed origin. Equivalent to mat (“tired”) + -en (infinitival suffix).

gloss: To nap or doze; to have a short sleep.
etymology: Inherited from Old English hnappian, from Proto-West Germanic *hnappōn, of unknown origin.

From pe, po (“peacock”) + cok (“cock, rooster”), from Old English pāwa, pēa (“peafowl”), from Latin pāvō (“peacock”), of unknown origin; perhaps related to Tamil தோகை (tōkai, “peacock feather”), or imitative (compare Latin paupulō (“to call as a peacock”).

gloss: Each of the seven celestial bodies seen as moving relative to the rest of the stars: the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn.
etymology: From Old French planete, from Latin planeta, planetes, from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs, “wanderer”), from Ancient Greek πλανάω (planáō, “wander about, stray”), of unknown origin. Perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to wander, roam”).
Borrowed from Anglo-Norman quaille, from Frankish *kwakla. Of uncertain ultimate origin; see Latin quaccola and Frankish *hwahtlā.
From Old English sċēap, sċēp, from Proto-West Germanic *skāp, from Proto-Germanic *skēpą, of unknown origin.
Inherited from Old English *slēte, *slīete, from Proto-West Germanic *slautijā, from Proto-Germanic *slautijǭ, of unclear origin.

gloss: One who lacks wisdom, knowledge, or intelligence; a stupid person.
etymology: From Old English sot, sott, from Medieval Latin sottus, reinforced by Old French sot (“idiotic”), of obscure origin. Possibly an expressive interjection, similar to modern French zut! (“damn it!”).

gloss: To dart out; to strike out.
etymology: From Old English sperran, spirran, spyrran, of unknown ultimate origin, perhaps related to Old Norse sperrask (“to kick out”). Or, a romance borrowing, from Middle French esparer (“to kick”), from old Italian sparare (“to fling”).

gloss: An unknown broomlike flowering plant with medicinal uses (possibly spignel).
etymology: From Anglo-Norman spigurnel, spigurnelle, and Anglo-Latin spigurnella, further etymology unknown.

gloss: branch, shoot, or twig of a tree
etymology: From Old English *spræġ, sprei (found in place names such as that of Spreyton, England), of unknown origin.

gloss: to spit water from the mouth; to squirt
etymology: Of uncertain origin; probably onomatopoeic.

gloss: A door-sill; the bottom board of a door.
etymology: From Old English þresċold, þerxold, þrexwold, from Proto-Germanic *þreskwaþluz; the first element is akin to threschen, but the second is of disputed origin, and was identified with several different words in Middle English.

gloss: A toad (dry-skinned member of the order Anura)
etymology: From Old English *tāde, a shortening of tādie, tādiġe, of uncertain origin. Compared to Old Norse and modern Danish tudse (“toad”), but OED rejects this because the zero grade of ai is i, not u. Possibly from a common Proto-Germanic word *tod (“small”), compared to Proto-Germanic *tūdrijaz (“small, frail”) (modern English tidbit) or *taltōną (“to sway, dangle, hesitate”) (modern English toddle), r

gloss: warren (breeding zone for small animals, especially rabbits).
etymology: From Anglo-Norman warenne, variant of garenne, of disputed origin.
From Old English wīf, from Proto-West Germanic *wīb, from Proto-Germanic *wībą, of uncertain origin.

gloss: Used to form the (nominative/accusative) plural form of regular nouns.
etymology: From Old English -as (a-stem nominative/accusative plural suffix), of disputed origin.
From Old English Ēlīg, of unknown origin.

From Latin Pēgasus, from Ancient Greek Πήγασος (Pḗgasos), traditionally associated with πηγή (pēgḗ, “spring, fountain, fountain fed by a spring”), especially used to denote springs of Ocean, where Perseus killed Medusa, from whose blood Pegasus sprang. Some have dismissed this as folk etymology and suggest a pre-Greek origin because of the -ασος suffix. First attested in the 14th century.

gloss: A fabric container; a bag, sack, pouch, purse, or wallet.
etymology: Usually taken to be borrowed from Old Norse baggi; perhaps reinforced by Old French bague, both of unknown etymology. However, some hypothesise derivation from a Old English *bagga (“badger, bag”), which alongside forms such as Middle Dutch bagghe (“piglet”) would be cognate to baggi.
Of unknown origin. Possibly onomatopoeic. Compare English mwa, mwah (“the sound made by a kiss”). Compare also Old French baisier (“to kiss”).

gloss: beet (plant of the genus Beta or its root or leaves)
etymology: Despite the gap in attestation, apparently inherited from Old English bēte, from Proto-West Germanic *bētā, from Latin bēta, of unknown origin.
Borrowed from Old French blason, of unknown origin.

From Old English brūcan, from Proto-West Germanic *brūkan, from Proto-Germanic *brūkaną.
The variant form with /oː/ (which is the source of the modern pronunciation) is of unclear origin.
Borrowed from Middle French bufet (“side table”), from Old French bufet, of unknown origin.
Possibly inherited from Old English calwer (“curds”), of unknown origin. The development of /lw/ to /lv/ before /r/ would be unparalleled, but there are no clear counterexamples either.

From Middle Irish crec, from Middle Irish carrac, possibly from the late Proto-Indo-European/substrate *kar (“stone, hard”); see also Old Armenian քար (kʻar, “stone”), Sanskrit खर (khara, “hard, solid”), Welsh carreg (“stone”).
Inherited from Old English culter, from Latin culter, of unclear origin. Forms with final /ə/ may be due to influence from Old French coutre or due to an Old English ō-stem by-form.

gloss: To prepare or ready:; To ornament, adorn.
etymology: From Old English dihtan, dihtian (“to set in order; dispose; arrange; appoint; direct; compose”), from Proto-Germanic *dihtōną (“to compose; invent”), of disputed origin.
Of obscure and uncertain origin. Probably cognate with Icelandic drukna.
From Old English fyrs, fyres, of unknown origin, but compare fyr (“fire”) and Proto-Slavic *pyrь (“couch grass”).
From Old English flītan, from Proto-West Germanic *flītan, of uncertain etymology.

gloss: A rushen basket for picking dried fruit; a frail.
etymology: Borrowed from Old French frael, fraiel, of unknown origin; possibly a dissimilatory variant of flael, flaiel (“flail”); if so, a doublet of fleyl.
Borrowed from Old French frette (“ring, loop”), of unclear origin; compare freten (“to bind”).
Borrowed from Old French graal, greal, from Medieval Latin gradālis (“dish”), of unknown origin.
From Anglo-Norman haie, of uncertain origin.
Inherited from Old English helde, of unknown origin.
Borrowed from Old French ahuge, a form of ahoge, of unknown origin.
Of obscure origin.

gloss: Any dried stem of a plant with a hollow interior.
etymology: Unknown. Possibly from a Celtic and/or substrate language.

gloss: Unrelated to the church; non-priestly; lay.
etymology:
From Old English lǣwede. According to the OED, of uncertain origin, but probably from Vulgar Latin *laigo-, from Late Latin laicus (“of the people”) + Old English -ede.
Otherwise, formally resembling a derivative of the past participle of Old English lǣwan (“to reveal, betray”) in the sense of "exposed as being unlearned" or "easily betrayed, clueless", from Proto-West Germanic *lāwijan (“to betra

From Old English lǣwede. According to the OED, of uncertain origin, but probably from Vulgar Latin *laigo-, from Late Latin laicus (“of the people”) + Old English -ede.
Otherwise, formally resembling a derivative of the past participle of Old English lǣwan (“to reveal, betray”) in the sense of "exposed as being unlearned" or "easily betrayed, clueless", from Proto-West Germanic *lāwijan (“to betra
From Old English lōma, of unknown origin.
Borrowed from Old French lovier, lover, from Medieval Latin *lōdārium (attested as lōvārium), extension of lōdium, of unclear origin.
Borrowed from Old French maquerel. Further origin unknown.

gloss: to mangle; to mutilate; to maim
etymology: From Old English mancian, bemancian (“to maim, mutilate”), of obscure origin. Cognate with Middle Low German mank (“lame, defective”), Dutch mank (“lame, defective”), and Middle High German manc (“lack, defect”). Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *mancāre, from Latin mancus (“maimed, crippled, frail, incomplete”), from Proto-Indo-European *mank-, *menk- (“maimed, mutilation, torment”).
From Old French moiste, of unknown origin.
From Old French moiste, of unknown origin.

gloss: mullein (a herb of the genus Verbascum)
etymology: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman moleine, of unclear origin.
From Anglo-Norman musherum, moscheron, of obscure origin.

gloss: To muse; to ponder:; To muse upon an object.
etymology: From Old French muser, of uncertain further origin.
From Latin opacus (“shaded, shady, dark”) (of unknown origin), later reinforced from Middle French opaque.
From Middle French petit, from Old French petit, from Vulgar Latin pittitus, of disputed origin.

From Middle Dutch pekel, Middle Low German pekel (“brine”). Of uncertain ultimate origin: Watkins suggests a connection with Proto-West Germanic *pikkōn (“to strike, peck”) (or perhaps the closely related Latin *picco (“I sting”)); Klein suggests derivation from a personal name of someone who perfected pickling.
Probably borrowed from Old French bodin, boudin, of disputed origin; the ending has apparently been remodelled after -ing.
Perhaps from Middle Dutch poken or Middle Low German poken, both from Proto-West Germanic *pukōn or similar, which is itself of uncertain origin.
From Old English pullian (“to pull, draw, tug, pluck off”), of uncertain ultimate origin.
Of uncertain origin; perhaps borrowed from Middle Dutch ratelen or of native origin related to Old English hratele, hrætele (“a plant known for its rustling or rattling sound”), ultimately imitative.
Borrowed from Old French reaume, of disputed origin. For the change of /ɛu̯/ to /ɛː/ before /m/, compare flewme.

gloss: A riot or uprising; a disturbance of the peace.
etymology: Borrowed from Anglo-Norman riot, riote, of unknown origin.
Borrowed from Anglo-Norman sauscistre (“sausage”), of unclear origin; compare Medieval Latin salsīstrum, salsīstra.

gloss: To avoid, spurn or eschew:; To refuse or deny; to spurn a request.
etymology: Inherited from Old English sċunian, sċynian, of unclear origin; possibly derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- and ultimately identical to Sanskrit स्कुनाति (skunāti, “to cover”).

gloss: To despise or revile; to view contemptuously.
etymology:
Borrowed from Old Northern French escarnir and central Old French escharnir, from Late Latin *scarnīre, *scernīre, of disputed origin. Derivation or influence from Old French or Middle French escornir (“to dehorn”, figuratively "to abase") is unlikely since that verb's figurative senses appear significantly later than scornen while failing to entirely approach its semantics. Compare scurnen.
Notes
Of uncertain origin; see English shark.
From Old English sot, sott, from Medieval Latin sottus, reinforced by Old French sot (“idiotic”), of obscure origin. Possibly an expressive interjection, similar to modern French zut! (“damn it!”).
Of unknown origin; the form points to an Old English *sugian; compare sorg (“sorrow, grief”).
Of uncertain origin. Perhaps from the Middle English verb spald (“to split”) (c.1400), from Middle Low German spalden, cognate with Old High German spaltan (“to split”).
From Anglo-Norman esparpeler (compare Old French esparpeillier), of unknown origin.
Of uncertain origin. Compare stabben.

gloss: a varnish that underlies gold or silver leaf
etymology: Of unclear origin; related to Old Italian sisa; perhaps ultimately related to syse (“amount”). See size for more.
From Old French tache (“stain, spot”), of uncertain origin; perhaps a native derivation, or borrowed from Gothic.
Borrowed from Old French tanesie, taneseie, from Early Medieval Latin tanacētum, atanacētum, of unclear origin.
Inherited from Old English *temes, from Proto-West Germanic *tamisu, of unclear origin.

gloss: A chest or casket; a strongbox.
etymology: Inherited from Old English tēag (“chest, enclosure”), of unclear origin; but possibly ultimately a semantic development of Etymology 1. A connection to Old Norse teigr (“plot of land”) is semantically attractive, though phonologically difficult.
From Old English tīþian, tiġþian, of unknown origin.
From Old French tresce, of unclear origin.
Borrowed from Middle Dutch tubbe or Middle Low German tubbe, tobbe, further etymology unknown.
From Old English wann (“dark”), from Proto-West Germanic *wann, from Proto-Germanic *wannaz, of uncertain origin.
Of obscure origin. Possibly from Old English *ġēamann, related to Old Frisian gāmann (“villager”), Middle Dutch goyman (“arbitrator”).
